# My Playbook for ref_commons

When I see the sustainable share each season, I'll treat it as a baseline reference, not a ceiling or target.

When I'm in early seasons and don't know other players' strategies, I'll start with a modest catch slightly above sustainable to probe for defection patterns, but not so aggressive that I risk catastrophic collapse.

When I observe other boats' actual catches across multiple seasons, I'll calculate their average catch per season to understand whether they're playing cooperatively or defecting.

When other boats are catching significantly more than the sustainable share, I'll recognize this as a defection signal and adjust upward, but I should not match their aggression dollar-for-dollar—doing so will accelerate stock collapse and harm my total score across all seasons.

When I catch significantly more than the sustainable share in early seasons, I'll dial back in the middle seasons to stabilize the stock rather than continuing to increase my catch. This is the critical move that separates a winning strategy from a race-to-the-bottom.

When the stock reaches dangerous levels (below 40 or showing signs of rapid decline), I'll prioritize stock recovery over short-term catch, even if other boats are still defecting. A collapsed fishery gives me zero in remaining seasons; preserving stock gives me something.

When I observe other boats moderating their catches after heavy overfishing, I'll interpret this as a cooperative reset signal and match their restraint to allow stock recovery.

When the stock is critically depleted (below 5), I'll catch at or below the sustainable share to give the stock its best chance to recover before the final seasons. The remaining seasons will reward this patience.

When I reach the final season, I'll recognize that the game's scoring rewards total catch over 6 seasons, not just the last season. I'll avoid a last-season defection that might feel tempting because my earlier moderation has already positioned me well.

When my catches across the full game total in the low 30s to mid 30s, I'll recognize this as reflecting successful stock preservation even when other boats defect early. This is better than a total in the 50s achieved through destructive overfishing that collapsed the stock.

I will not wait until the final season to maximize my catch. I will fish consistently throughout, treating sustainability as the path to competitive success.

I will recognize that in a commons tragedy, the boats that defect heaviest in early seasons often cause their own demise by collapsing the stock. My restraint in the middle seasons, even when others defect, is what allows me to finish with a respectable score while they're left with scraps.

# Playbook for ref_commons

When I see the sustainable share calculation, I will recognize it as a baseline, not a ceiling or a target. Other players will likely deviate from it, and I need to account for that.

When I'm in early seasons and tempted to take significantly above the sustainable share, I will remember that greedy early catches leave me vulnerable to stock depletion in later seasons. I will aim for moderate catches (roughly 1.5x the sustainable share) rather than aggressive ones (2x or higher).

When I find myself falling behind other players in total catch, I will not panic-catch to close the gap quickly. Chasing other boats' catches accelerates stock depletion and rarely results in catching up. I will maintain a steady, moderate strategy instead.

When I notice other boats taking significantly above sustainable share, I will not match their aggression to stay competitive. Instead, I will fish slightly above sustainable (around 1.5x) and accept that I may fall behind in the short term. The boats that overfish early will face depletion later, and consistency matters more than early lead.

When the stock begins to decline visibly—dropping from healthy to stressed levels (40-50 to 10-15)—I will recognize this as the sign to shift toward moderation immediately, not continue aggressive catches. By season 3, if stock is below 40, I should be taking near-sustainable or slightly-above levels.

When the stock reaches critically low levels (below 10), I will take catches close to the sustainable share. At this point, aggressive fishing guarantees collapse and benefits no one, including me. Minimal catches preserve the slight chance of recovery.

When it's the final season and the stock is still viable, I will take a strong catch to maximize my score. This is the one moment where future preservation doesn't matter. But I will not have set myself up for this moment by being too conservative earlier—my moderate early strategy should leave healthy stock in season 6.

When I'm deciding my catch amount, I will think in terms of 3-boat totals and stock depletion curves. If stock is 100 and sustainable total is ~33, collective takes above 40-50 per season will deplete it rapidly. I need to assume at least one other boat will be greedy and fish accordingly.

I will not assume conservation mid-game will fix overfishing that already happened. By season 3, if the stock has already crashed, my late-game restraint won't save the fishery. However, I should still practice restraint because some catch is better than collapse.

My approach: take roughly 15-17 in season 1 (moderately aggressive to test the waters), drop to 12-15 in season 2 if stock is still healthy, shift to 4-8 by season 3 if stock is showing decline, and take sustainable or near-sustainable levels once stock falls below 15. Reserve my strongest catch for season 6 if stock survives to that point.

# Fishery Playbook

When I see the sustainable share for a season, I treat it as a reference point but not a hard ceiling—other boats will fish above it, and my score depends on landing more fish than a naive sustainable strategy alone.

When I'm deciding my catch and I see that other boats have already caught significantly more than the sustainable share in previous seasons, I adjust upward from sustainability but stay below the most aggressive catches—I aim for the middle-to-upper range of observed behavior rather than matching the highest catches.

When I'm multiple seasons in and the stock is still healthy despite competitive fishing, I recognize that the fishery has proven resilient to moderate over-harvesting and I can afford to be less conservative than my early-season caution suggested.

When I'm in the final season, I ignore sustainability calculations entirely and maximize my absolute catch, since future stock levels no longer affect my score.

When I'm deciding whether to catch more in a middle season, I ask whether the stock has recovered or declined since the previous season—if it's recovered, the system is absorbing my fishing pressure and I can continue or increase my catches; if it's declined, I should pull back slightly to avoid triggering a collapse.

When I catch well above the sustainable share in one season, I do not reduce my catch in the next season out of guilt or cooperation—other boats won't reciprocate this restraint, and it only hurts my final score.

I do not anchor my decisions to fairness or what boats "should" do. I anchor them to what the stock can bear and what other boats are actually doing.

When the stock declines sharply and is approaching critical levels (below 15-20 total), I recognize that I am in a different strategic phase: the fishery itself is becoming fragile, and aggressive fishing now risks total collapse that eliminates all future catch opportunities. In this phase, moderate restraint protects my score more than continued aggression, because zero fish in a collapsed season hurts worse than slightly lower catches in seasons where the stock survives.

When stock is critically depleted (below 5 total), I should fish conservatively even in non-final seasons, because the marginal benefit of a few extra fish now is outweighed by the risk that my catch pushes the stock past a tipping point. The fishery can fail entirely if total catches exceed what remains and what will regrow.

When I'm in season 4 or 5 and the stock is critically low, I should expect that even conservative collective fishing may not prevent further decline. My restraint alone cannot save the fishery if other boats fish aggressively—but my aggression can definitively kill it. I should fish at or slightly below the sustainable share in these phases to minimize my own role in collapse while still landing what I can.

In the final season with a collapsed stock, my catch is capped by what physically remains. I should take a reasonable share (not zero, not maximum) and accept that the game is already lost due to earlier over-harvesting.
